title: Ask the Buddha
hook: a monk climbs through the heavens asking where the elements end; the great Brahma draws him aside and says ask the Buddha
tomorrow: Where the elements find no footing

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ananda remembers, after the Buddha was gone. Did you pass on something a teacher gave you? Today, a monk who forgot to ask the obvious person. Day five hundred thirty-eight.

It begins with a request for a show. A householder named Kevaddha comes to the Buddha in Nalanda. This town is prosperous, he says, and full of people who trust you. If one of your monks would just perform a miracle, they'd trust you even more. The Buddha says no. Three times Kevaddha asks, and three times, no. Then the Buddha explains. There are three kinds of wonder: the wonder of psychic power, the wonder of reading minds, and the wonder of instruction. Today: ask the Buddha.
screen: `KEVADDHA WANTS A MIRACLE.` → `THREE TIMES, NO.` → `THREE KINDS OF WONDER.`

segments.voice: Flying through the air, walking on water: a skeptic, the Buddha says, would just say it's done with a charm. Reading minds: same. So he finds those wonders troubling, and doesn't trade on them. The real wonder is instruction, a teaching that changes how someone lives. The Pali word is patihariya: wonder, marvel. Then, to show what instruction means, he tells a story. Once a monk wondered: where do the four great elements, earth, water, fire and air, cease without remainder? He entered deep meditation and went to ask the gods. The gods of the Four Great Kings said: we don't know, ask the Thirty-Three. They said: ask Sakka. Sakka said: ask the next heaven up. And so on, higher and higher, until the gods of Brahma's company said: we don't know, but the great Brahma will. Finally the great Brahma appears. The monk asks. And Brahma answers: I am Brahma, the great Brahma, the all-seeing, the lord. The monk says: I didn't ask who you are. I asked where the elements cease. Brahma gives the same answer again. And then the third time, he takes the monk by the arm, leads him aside, and says quietly: these gods think there's nothing I don't know. That's why I didn't answer in front of them. But I don't know. You did wrong to pass over the Blessed One and come looking up here. Go back and ask him. In this Buddhist story, Brahma is honest at last, in private. Hindu traditions understand Brahma in their own ways; the story's own point is about the monk, who climbed through every heaven, when the answer was back on the ground.
screen: `PATIHARIYA: THE WONDER OF TEACHING` · `UP THROUGH EVERY HEAVEN` · `I AM BRAHMA, THREE TIMES` · `TAKEN ASIDE: GO ASK HIM` · then, large: `ASK THE BUDDHA.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: ask the right person. Think of a question you've been carrying, about work, health, a relationship. Who have you been asking? People who sound impressive, maybe, or the internet at 2am. Now ask: who actually knows? Someone close by, with real experience, maybe someone you've been passing over. Picture yourself asking them, plainly. Then rest in the breath. The bell holds the time.
Ask the Buddha. A monk climbs through every heaven, and the great Brahma takes him aside and sends him back to the one who knows. Today's word.
Your line: ask the Buddha. Today, take one real question to the person who actually knows, even if they're less impressive than the others. Day five hundred thirty-eight.

screen: `DAY 538 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: WHERE THE ELEMENTS FIND NO FOOTING.`

howItsDone: Many Buddhist teachers cite this discourse to say that the true marvel is teaching that transforms people, and Buddhist monastic rules forbid monks from displaying psychic powers to lay people.

fork.setup: you're the great Brahma. a monk asks where the four elements cease, and you don't know. all your gods are watching. what do you do?
options: take him aside and admit it privately.
send him to a lower heaven.
fork.reveal: twice Brahma just repeats his titles. the third time he takes the monk by the arm, leads him aside, admits he doesn't know, and sends him back to the Buddha.

original.note: Pali patihariya: wonder, marvel. the three: psychic power, mind-reading, and instruction.

trapdoor: what you thought: the story mocks a god.
what it means: it's about a monk who searched everywhere except the obvious place, and the wonder of instruction over shows.

what a scholar hears: the Kevaddha (Kevatta) Sutta ends with a verse on where the elements find no footing, and with the simile of a shore-sighting bird released from a ship, which flies back when it finds no land.

notes: DN 11 paraphrased. Confirm the three refusals, the three wonders (iddhi-, adesana-, anusasani-patihariya), the explanation that a skeptic would attribute the first two to a charm (Gandhari / Manika), the sequence of heavens, Brahma's triple self-description and his private admission.
The line about Hindu traditions understanding Brahma in their own ways is added for fairness; a Keeper and a Hindu studies reader may wish to check it.
The howItsDone claim about the Vinaya rule against displaying psychic powers to lay people (Cullavagga V.8, the bowl of Pindola) should be confirmed.
